Yes, you're right, and it isn't pedantry: the two numbers can differ by an order of magnitude.

A p-value of 0.03 is P(data at least this extreme | H0). The "97% true" claim is a statement about P(hypothesis | data), which also requires a prior. Even in the most favorable case, the gap is large: with a 50/50 prior, the Sellke-Bayarri-Berger bound (minimum Bayes factor ≈ -e·p·ln p ≈ 0.29) leaves H0 with at least ~22% posterior probability, not 3%. If the hypothesis was a long shot to begin with (typical in exploratory work), the posterior probability of H0 can be far higher still.

The practical consequence is that your colleague's reading will systematically overstate evidence, and it's the main reason p ≈ 0.03 results replicate less often than people expect.
